items.stem: Wet oxidation grows silicon dioxide considerably faster than dry oxidation at the same temperature. What is the underlying reason?

options.text: Water vapour dissolves into the oxide at a much higher equilibrium concentration than oxygen does
Water vapour reacts with silicon at a lower activation energy, so the interface reaction is faster
The hydrogen released during wet growth physically opens channels through the oxide
Wet oxidation runs at higher furnace pressure

steps: Both ambients have to get oxidant through the oxide already grown before any new oxide can form.
The rate that transport supports depends on $C^{*}$, the equilibrium concentration of oxidant dissolved in the oxide — Henry's law applied at the surface.
$C^{*}$ for $\mathrm{H_2O}$ is roughly three orders of magnitude larger than for $\mathrm{O_2}$, so far more oxidant per unit time reaches the interface.
That shows up in the model as a much larger $B$ — wet growth is faster because more oxidant is available to diffuse, not because the reaction is easier.
explanation.principle: Both rate constants trace back to a physical step. B is about transport through the oxide; B/A is about the reaction at the interface.
hints: Which of the two rate constants differs most between wet and dry?
What has to happen before oxidant can react at all?

items.stem: Gate oxides are grown dry even though dry oxidation is much slower. Why is the slower process preferred here?

options.text: Dry oxide is denser and carries fewer traps and defects, which a thin gate dielectric cannot tolerate
Dry oxide grows more uniformly across the wafer than wet oxide
Wet oxidation cannot produce films thin enough for a gate
Dry oxidation consumes less silicon per unit of oxide grown

steps: A gate oxide is the thinnest and most electrically stressed film on the wafer: it must hold off a field near $10^{7}\ \mathrm{V/cm}$ and must not trap charge.
Wet growth incorporates hydrogen and leaves a more open network, which shows up as a higher defect and trap density.
Dry growth is slower precisely because less oxidant is available, and the film it leaves is denser and more nearly stoichiometric.
Being slow is acceptable when the target is only a few nanometres, so dry is the right trade for a gate and the wrong one for a field oxide.
explanation.principle: Growth rate and film quality pull in opposite directions, and which one matters is decided by what the oxide is for.
hints: What is a gate oxide asked to do electrically?
Is growth time a real cost at gate-oxide thicknesses?

items.stem: The Deal-Grove derivation sets three fluxes equal and then discards the first. What assumption justifies dropping the gas-phase flux $F_1$?

options.text: The ambient is well mixed, so the oxidant concentration at the oxide surface stays at its equilibrium value
The gas-phase flux is negligible because gases diffuse slowly compared with solids
$F_1$ is already included in the parabolic rate constant $B$
The furnace is evacuated, so there is no gas phase to transport through

steps: Gas-phase transport to the wafer is fast compared with diffusion through a solid oxide and with the interface reaction.
So the surface concentration never becomes depleted: $C_0$ stays pinned at the Henry's-law value $C^{*}$.
With $C_0 = C^{*}$ fixed, $F_1$ carries no information and drops out of the analysis.
This is why gas flow rate, wafer spacing and wafer orientation in the boat have essentially no effect on growth rate — a prediction the model makes and experiment confirms.
explanation.principle: A flux that is never rate-limiting can be removed from a steady-state chain without changing the answer. Deciding which one that is, is most of the modelling.
hints: Which of the three steps is fastest?
What would have to be true for gas flow rate to matter?

items.stem: Why does the linear rate constant $B/A$ depend on substrate crystal orientation while the parabolic constant $B$ does not?

options.text: $B/A$ is set by the interface reaction, which depends on available bond sites; $B$ is set by diffusion through an amorphous film that has no lattice
$B$ does depend on orientation, but the dependence is too weak to tabulate
$B/A$ varies because thin oxides are partly crystalline and inherit the substrate lattice
Orientation changes the oxide density, which changes the linear constant only

steps: $B/A = k_s C^{*}/N_1$ is governed by $k_s$, the rate of the reaction at the silicon surface.
That reaction consumes silicon atoms at the interface, so its rate depends on how densely those atoms are packed on the exposed plane — $(111)$ is the densest and reacts fastest.
$B = 2DC^{*}/N_1$ is governed by $D$, the diffusivity of oxidant through the oxide already grown.
That oxide is amorphous, so it has no orientation to inherit and $D$ cannot depend on the substrate plane. Correct $B/A$ for orientation and never $B$.
explanation.principle: Each rate constant inherits the symmetry of the physical step behind it. Amorphous films forget the lattice they grew on.
hints: Which constant describes something happening at the silicon surface?
Is the grown oxide crystalline?

items.stem: A thick oxide is being grown. Which step limits the growth rate, and what does the thickness-time relationship look like?

options.text: Diffusion of oxidant through the existing oxide; thickness goes as the square root of time
The interface reaction; thickness goes linearly with time
Gas-phase supply of oxidant; thickness saturates
Silicon consumption at the interface; thickness goes as the cube root of time

steps: Once the oxide is thick, an oxidant molecule spends most of its journey crossing it, and that crossing is the slow step.
In that limit the $x_0/(B/A)$ term is small beside $x_0^2/B$, so $x_0^2 \approx Bt$.
Hence $x_0 \approx \sqrt{Bt}$, and $B$ is called the parabolic rate constant because $x_0^2$ is linear in $t$.
The opposite limit — a very thin oxide — is reaction-limited and gives $x_0 \approx (B/A)t$, linear in time.
explanation.principle: The same quadratic contains both regimes. Which term dominates is a statement about how far the oxidant has to travel.
hints: Which term in the quadratic grows faster as the oxide thickens?
Why is B called parabolic?

items.stem: Converting silicon to silicon dioxide expands the volume by about 2.2 times. Where does that extra volume go?

options.text: Upward: the oxide grows into the ambient, so about 56% of the film stands above the original silicon surface
Laterally, which is why oxide spreads under a nitride mask
Nowhere — the oxide is compressed to the volume of the silicon it replaced
Downward into the substrate, so the wafer thickens

steps: The wafer is laterally constrained and rigid, so the only low-stress direction available to a growing film is normal to the surface.
Oxidation consumes silicon from below the original surface while depositing a film 2.2 times that volume.
The arithmetic gives the familiar split: 44% of the finished oxide thickness lies below the original surface and 56% above it.
A cross-section question is always this split applied to each region of the wafer separately.
explanation.principle: Oxide does not sit on silicon; it replaces some of it and expands. Every recess and step-height calculation follows from that.
hints: Which direction is unconstrained?
If 44% of the oxide came from below the surface, where is the rest?

items.stem: A nitride mask patterned on pad oxide produces a "bird's beak" at the edge of a LOCOS field oxide. What causes it?

options.text: Oxidant diffuses laterally through the pad oxide under the nitride edge, growing oxide that lifts the mask
The nitride shrinks during the high-temperature step and exposes silicon at its edge
Photoresist rounding transfers a tapered edge into the nitride
Silicon diffuses out from under the mask and oxidises in the field region

steps: Nitride blocks oxidant, but the pad oxide beneath it does not — it is silicon dioxide, the very medium oxidant diffuses through.
So oxidant arrives sideways under the mask edge and grows oxide there.
That oxide expands, prying the nitride edge upward and producing the tapering wedge the cross-section shows.
The result is lost area at every isolation edge, which is why LOCOS was eventually replaced by shallow trench isolation.
explanation.principle: A mask stops what lands on it, not what arrives from the side. Lateral transport under a mask edge limits every masked thermal process.
hints: Is the pad oxide a barrier to oxidant?
What would make the nitride edge lift?

items.stem: Why is a purge gas flowed through an oxidation furnace during loading, unloading and temperature ramps?

options.text: To displace air and moisture so no uncontrolled oxide grows outside the intended process step
To cool the wafers quickly enough to avoid thermal shock
To carry particles away from the wafer surface by entrainment
To maintain furnace pressure above atmospheric so contaminants cannot enter

steps: Silicon at furnace temperature oxidises in whatever oxygen or water vapour is present, whether or not the recipe has started.
An inert purge — nitrogen is the usual choice — displaces those species from the tube.
That keeps the grown thickness equal to what the recipe specifies rather than the recipe plus an uncontrolled contribution from loading.
The same reasoning applies on the way out: a hot wafer in air keeps growing oxide until it cools.
explanation.principle: Thermal processes do not start and stop with the recipe. Controlling the ambient is how the process is bounded in time.
hints: What is the wafer doing while it sits hot in air?
What property must the purge gas have?

items.stem: Heavily doped silicon oxidises faster than lightly doped silicon, and the effect is strongest for thin oxides. Why?

options.text: Heavy doping raises the vacancy concentration near the surface, and consuming a vacancy site is easier than breaking an intact Si–Si bond — which speeds the interface reaction
Dopant atoms dissolve into the oxide and raise the oxidant diffusivity through it
Heavy doping lowers the melting point, so the lattice is more reactive
Dopants react directly with oxygen to form their own oxides

steps: The interface reaction has to break silicon out of the lattice, and a site that is already a vacancy costs nothing to break.
Heavy doping — especially $n^{+}$ — raises the equilibrium vacancy concentration, so more such sites are available.
That accelerates $k_s$ and therefore $B/A$, the linear constant.
Because $B/A$ dominates only while the oxide is thin, the effect is pronounced in the linear regime and fades once growth becomes diffusion-limited.
explanation.principle: An effect on one rate constant only shows up in the regime that constant controls. Knowing which regime is affected is half of knowing the mechanism.
hints: Which rate constant describes the surface reaction?
In which thickness regime does that constant dominate?

items.stem: Ellipsometry and reflectometry both measure oxide thickness. What does ellipsometry provide that reflectometry does not?

options.text: The optical constants of the film as well as its thickness, because it measures the polarisation change on reflection
A thickness measurement that does not require the film to be transparent
Measurement without contacting the wafer
Better lateral resolution across the wafer

steps: Reflectometry measures reflected intensity against wavelength and fits a thickness to the interference pattern.
Ellipsometry measures how the polarisation state changes on reflection, which carries two independent quantities rather than one.
That lets it solve for the refractive index $n$ and extinction coefficient $k$ alongside the thickness.
Both are non-contact and optical; the difference is how many unknowns the measurement can support.
explanation.principle: What a measurement can determine is bounded by how many independent quantities it records.
hints: How many numbers does each technique actually measure?
What else besides thickness sets a film's reflectance?

items.stem: What is the purpose of adding a chlorine-bearing species such as HCl to the oxygen flow during thermal oxidation?

options.text: To convert mobile alkali ions into volatile chlorides that leave with the exhaust, gettering them during growth
To increase the oxidation rate by raising the oxidant concentration
To etch back the oxide continuously and improve thickness uniformity
To passivate dangling bonds at the silicon surface

steps: Sodium and potassium are the classic mobile charges in $\mathrm{SiO_2}$: they drift under gate bias and shift threshold voltage over time.
Chlorine present during growth binds them as volatile chlorides, which are carried away rather than incorporated.
This is gettering performed in situ, during the oxidation, rather than as a separate step.
It does modestly increase the growth rate as a side effect, but that is not why it is done.
explanation.principle: Contamination control is not only a separate cleaning step; some process steps are arranged to reject contaminants while they run.
hints: Which impurities move under bias in an oxide?
What would make such an impurity leave the furnace?

items.stem: Gate dielectrics moved to high-$k$ materials once oxide thicknesses approached one nanometre. What problem forced the change?

options.text: Direct quantum-mechanical tunnelling through the gate dielectric, which rises steeply as the film thins
The oxide could no longer be grown uniformly at those thicknesses
The dielectric constant of $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ falls at very small thicknesses
Dopant atoms began to diffuse through the oxide into the channel

steps: Scaling demands more gate capacitance per unit area, which for a fixed material means a thinner film.
Below roughly one to two nanometres, carriers tunnel directly through the dielectric and gate leakage becomes a significant share of total power.
A higher-permittivity material reaches the same capacitance with a physically thicker film, and tunnelling depends on physical thickness.
The film is then quoted as an equivalent oxide thickness: a 4 nm high-$k$ layer can present an EOT near 1 nm while leaking far less.
explanation.principle: Equivalent oxide thickness separates the electrical requirement from the physical one. High-k exists to let those two diverge.
hints: What happens to a barrier as it gets thin?
Does tunnelling care about electrical or physical thickness?

items.stem: Airborne particles between roughly 10 nm and 10 µm are the hardest to remove from fab air. Why are particles outside that band easier?

options.text: Smaller particles coagulate into larger ones that filter readily, and larger particles settle out under gravity before reaching a wafer
Particles outside that band are electrically neutral and are captured by ionisers
HEPA filters are designed to pass that band and trap everything else
Only particles in that band are generated inside the fab

steps: Very small particles undergo strong Brownian motion, collide often and stick together, so they quickly become larger particles that filters capture.
Very large particles have enough mass that gravitational settling removes them from the air on a short timescale.
The intermediate band does neither efficiently: too large to coagulate quickly, too small to settle quickly.
So it stays suspended and airborne, which is exactly the population that can drift down onto a wafer.
explanation.principle: Removal mechanisms have opposite size dependences, so the hardest case is always somewhere in the middle.
hints: What happens to very small particles over time?
What removes large particles without any equipment?

items.stem: The RCA sequence uses several different chemistries rather than one bath. What makes the sequence necessary?

options.text: No single chemistry removes organics, native oxide, transition metals and alkali ions, so each step targets a different contaminant class
Repeated exposure to one chemistry would etch the silicon too deeply
Mixing the chemistries in one bath would be explosive
Each step has to run at a different temperature, which one bath cannot provide

steps: Organic residues need a strong oxidiser to break them up, which is what the sulphuric-peroxide step supplies.
Native and chemical oxide needs dilute HF, which nothing else strips selectively.
Particles and the noble and transition metals come off in the ammonia-peroxide step; alkali ions and the remaining metals need the acidic hydrochloric-peroxide step.
The classes are chemically unlike each other, so the sequence is a sequence by necessity rather than by tradition.
explanation.principle: A clean is defined by what it has to remove. Four unlike contaminant classes require four unlike chemistries.
hints: Name the contaminant classes present on an incoming wafer.
Would an acid that strips oxide also break up an organic film?

items.stem: For a metallic contaminant to be rinsed off a wafer, what has to happen to it first, and why?

options.text: It must be oxidised to an ion, because only a soluble ionic species will dissolve into the bath and leave with the rinse
It must be reduced to its metallic state so it no longer bonds to silicon
It must be driven into the bulk where the rinse can reach it
It must be covered by oxide so it lifts off when the oxide is stripped

steps: A neutral metal atom on the surface is not soluble in water and will simply stay there, or re-plate if it does leave.
Oxidising it, $M \rightarrow M^{+} + e^{-}$, produces a charged species that water solvates.
Whether a given bath can do this is set by the relative oxidation-reduction potentials: the bath has to be the stronger oxidiser.
Hydrogen peroxide is what supplies that oxidising power in both RCA steps; a plain water rinse would let iron plate back onto the surface instead.
explanation.principle: Cleaning is a solubility problem before it is a rinsing problem. The chemistry exists to make the contaminant soluble.
hints: Is a metal atom soluble in water?
What does the peroxide contribute that water does not?

items.stem: Gettering is described as free, diffuse and trap. Why must the freeing step come first?

options.text: A metal sitting substitutionally in the lattice is effectively immobile; it must be kicked into an interstitial site before it can diffuse anywhere
The trap sites do not exist until a high-temperature step creates them
The metal must be oxidised before it will move
Freeing lowers the metal concentration enough for diffusion to begin

steps: Gettering works by moving contaminants from where devices are to somewhere harmless, which requires them to move at all.
Substitutional metals are bound into lattice sites and diffuse extremely slowly.
A high-temperature step promotes them into interstitial sites, where metals diffuse quickly.
Only then can the second step — diffusion toward the gettering sites — happen on a practical timescale, with trapping as the third.
explanation.principle: Each step in a three-step mechanism enables the next. The ordering is the mechanism, not a convention.
hints: How fast does a substitutional metal diffuse?
What has to be true before a diffusion step can work?

items.stem: Gettering fails when the contamination level is too high. What breaks down?

options.text: The available trap sites saturate, and once they are full there is nothing to hold further contaminant
High contamination lowers the diffusivity so contaminants cannot reach the traps
Excess contaminant reacts with the getter layer and destroys it
The denuded zone collapses at high contamination levels

steps: Gettering sites are a finite population of damaged regions, precipitates or heavily doped volumes.
Each one can immobilise a limited amount of contaminant.
Once they are occupied, further contaminant has nowhere to go and remains in the active region regardless of how long the anneal runs.
Gettering is therefore a finishing technique for a clean process, not a substitute for one.
explanation.principle: A sink with finite capacity only helps while it has capacity. Contamination control is upstream of gettering, not replaced by it.
hints: What physically holds the contaminant at a gettering site?
Is that capacity unlimited?

items.stem: What distinguishes intrinsic gettering from extrinsic gettering?

options.text: Intrinsic gettering uses oxygen precipitates nucleated in the wafer bulk; extrinsic gettering uses damage or layers deliberately introduced, usually at the backside
Intrinsic gettering happens during crystal growth; extrinsic gettering happens during device processing
Intrinsic gettering traps alkali ions; extrinsic gettering traps transition metals
Intrinsic gettering is permanent; extrinsic gettering reverses on cooling

steps: Czochralski silicon carries dissolved oxygen picked up from the quartz crucible during the pull.
A nucleation and growth anneal precipitates that oxygen deep in the bulk, and the strain around the precipitates traps metals — the traps come from the wafer itself, hence intrinsic.
A denuded zone is left near the surface, cleared of precipitates, so devices sit in good material while the traps sit safely below them.
Extrinsic gettering instead adds something: backside implant damage, abrasion, a polysilicon layer, or a phosphorus-rich glass.
explanation.principle: The distinction is where the trap sites come from, not what they catch.
hints: Where does the oxygen in a CZ wafer come from?
What is a denuded zone for?

items.stem: A particle that was harmless at an older technology node can be a killer defect at a newer one, without changing size. Why?

options.text: Killer size is relative to the minimum feature: as features shrink, a fixed particle becomes large enough to bridge or open a structure
Newer nodes use thinner films, which particles penetrate more easily
Newer processes run at lower temperatures, so particles are not annealed out
Particle composition changes as processes change

steps: A defect kills a die only if it actually breaks a circuit — shorting two conductors, or opening one.
Whether a given particle can do that depends on its size compared with the line width and spacing around it.
Shrinking the node shrinks that comparison length, so the critical defect size falls with it.
The particle population has not changed; the threshold moved, which is why particle targets keep tightening indefinitely.
explanation.principle: Defectivity requirements are set by a ratio, not an absolute size. That is why the target never stops moving.
hints: What makes a defect a killer rather than a nuisance?
Which quantity in that comparison changed?

items.stem: The Poisson yield model tends to underpredict the yield of large die. What assumption causes that?

options.text: It assumes defects are spatially uncorrelated, whereas real defects cluster — leaving more entirely defect-free die than the model expects
It assumes every defect is a killer defect
It ignores parametric failures, which dominate for large die
It assumes defect density is independent of die area

steps: Poisson treats each defect as landing independently and uniformly across the wafer.
Real defects arrive in clusters — a tool excursion, a handling scratch, an edge effect — so they concentrate on some die and spare others.
Clustering means more die escape entirely than independence would predict, so true yield exceeds the Poisson figure.
The negative binomial model adds a clustering factor $C$ to capture this, and recovers Poisson only in the limit of no clustering at all.
explanation.principle: A yield model is a statement about the spatial statistics of defects. Getting the statistics wrong biases the answer in a predictable direction.
hints: Do defects arrive independently in a real fab?
Does clustering help or hurt the number of clean die?

items.stem: In the negative binomial model $Y = (1 + A_c D_0/C)^{-C}$, what happens as the clustering factor $C$ becomes very large?

options.text: The model approaches the Poisson result, because large $C$ means little clustering
The model approaches the Poisson result, because $C$ tending to zero is the uncorrelated case
Yield approaches one regardless of defect density
Yield approaches the Seeds model

steps: Small $C$ means heavy clustering; the Seeds model is the $C = 1$ case and predicts the highest yield of the three.
As $C$ grows, clustering weakens and the predicted yield falls toward the uncorrelated case.
Taking the limit, $(1 + A_c D_0/C)^{-C} \to e^{-A_c D_0}$ as $C \to \infty$, which is exactly Poisson.
Setting $C = 0$ instead gives an indeterminate form and no limit at all, so the Poisson case is the large-$C$ end and not the small-$C$ end.
explanation.principle: The clustering factor runs from heavily clustered at small C to uncorrelated at large C, and Poisson sits at the uncorrelated end.
hints: Which end of the C range means no clustering?
Which model predicts the lowest yield at a given area?

items.stem: A process shows $C_p = 1.94$ but $C_{pk} = 1.60$. What does the gap between them say?

options.text: The spread is tight enough for the specification, but the mean is off centre — recentring would raise $C_{pk}$ without reducing variation at all
The distribution is not Gaussian, so the indices disagree
The variation is too large and must be reduced before the process can be capable
Measurement error is inflating one of the two indices

steps: $C_p$ compares the full specification width against $6\sigma$ and says nothing about where the distribution sits.
$C_{pk}$ measures the distance from the mean to the nearer specification limit in units of $3\sigma$, so it falls when the mean drifts off target.
The two are equal only when the mean sits exactly at the midpoint of the specification.
A high $C_p$ with a lower $C_{pk}$ therefore diagnoses a centring problem, which is usually cheaper to fix than a variation problem.
explanation.principle: Two indices that differ only in whether they notice the mean turn a single number into a diagnosis.
hints: Which index notices where the mean sits?
What would make the two indices equal?

items.stem: A voltage regulator comes off the line functional but delivers 2.9 V where the specification demands 3.3 V. How is this classified?

options.text: A parametric failure — the die works but falls outside its specified window
A functional failure, since the part does not meet its specification
A killer defect, since the die cannot be sold
A yield loss that no model accounts for

steps: A functional failure means the circuit does not do its job at all — a stuck node, a short, an open.
This part performs its function; it simply performs it outside the allowed range.
That is a parametric failure, and it traces to manufacturing variation, design margin, or both rather than to a particle.
It is exactly the loss mechanism $C_p$ and $C_{pk}$ are monitored to control, which is why process capability sits in the same unit as defect density.
explanation.principle: Yield loss splits into die that cannot work and die that work wrongly. The two have different causes and different remedies.
hints: Does the part perform its intended function?
Which yield mechanism does process capability address?

items.stem: What distinguishes a positive photoresist from a negative one?

options.text: In a positive resist exposure weakens the polymer and the developer removes the exposed regions; in a negative resist exposure cross-links it and the developer removes the unexposed regions
A positive resist is used for etch masks and a negative resist for implant masks
A positive resist requires a post-exposure bake and a negative one does not
A positive resist responds to shorter wavelengths than a negative resist

steps: Both resists change solubility on exposure; they differ in which direction.
A positive resist becomes more soluble where light landed, so the developed pattern reproduces the clear areas of the mask.
A negative resist cross-links where light landed and becomes less soluble, so the developed pattern is the mask's complement.
Reading a contrast curve tells you which you have: if resist remains at low dose and clears at high dose the resist is positive, and the reverse for negative.
explanation.principle: Polarity is about which regions survive development, which is what decides whether the printed image matches the mask or inverts it.
hints: Which regions does the developer remove in each case?
How would a contrast curve differ between the two?

items.stem: At which step of the lithography module does the catalytic amplification in a chemically amplified DUV resist actually occur?

options.text: The post-exposure bake — exposure only generates the initial acid, and heat drives the catalytic cascade
The exposure step itself, since that is where the photons arrive
The develop step, when the developer reaches the acid
The soft bake, which prepares the acid generator

steps: A photo-acid generator converts absorbed photons into a small quantity of acid during exposure.
That acid is a catalyst: it deprotects resin sites and is regenerated, so one acid molecule can alter many sites.
The cascade needs thermal energy to proceed, which is supplied by the post-exposure bake.
This is why chemically amplified resists reach quantum efficiencies above one, and why PEB timing and temperature are tightly controlled — it is a real reaction step, not a drying step.
explanation.principle: In a chemically amplified resist, exposure and chemical change happen at different steps. That separation is what buys the sensitivity.
hints: What does the exposure actually produce in a PAG resist?
What does a catalytic cascade need to run?

items.stem: How is the thickness of a spun-on photoresist film primarily controlled?

options.text: By spin speed, together with the viscosity and solids content of the resist
By the volume of resist dispensed onto the wafer
By the soft-bake temperature
By the duration of the dispense step

steps: Spin coating reaches a steady state in which centrifugal thinning balances viscous resistance and solvent evaporation.
That equilibrium sets the final thickness, and it depends on angular velocity and on the fluid itself.
Thickness falls roughly as the inverse square root of spin speed, so faster spinning gives a thinner film.
Dispense volume barely matters provided the wafer is fully wetted — the excess is flung off before the film sets.
explanation.principle: Spin coating is self-limiting: the film thins until the physics balances, so the endpoint depends on the spin and the fluid rather than on how much was poured.
hints: What balances what during a spin?
Does pouring twice as much resist give twice the thickness?

items.stem: Why do EUV lithography systems image with mirrors rather than lenses?

options.text: No material is transparent at 13.5 nm, so refractive optics are impossible and multilayer reflective optics are used instead
Mirrors can be made larger than lenses, giving a higher numerical aperture
Lenses would introduce chromatic aberration at EUV wavelengths
Mirrors tolerate the heat load from the plasma source better

steps: At 13.5 nm every material absorbs strongly, including the glasses used for DUV optics.
A lens requires light to pass through it, so refractive optics simply cannot be built at this wavelength.
Reflection is still possible using multilayer Bragg mirrors tuned to the wavelength, though each reflects only around 70%.
Because losses compound across a mirror stack, the whole system — including the mask, which is also reflective — has to work in vacuum with very few optical elements.
explanation.principle: The optics available at a wavelength are set by what materials do at that wavelength, and that constraint shapes the entire tool.
hints: What must be true of a material for a lens to work?
Is there any transparent material at 13.5 nm?

items.stem: Immersion lithography puts water between the final lens element and the wafer. What does it actually achieve?

options.text: It removes the refractive-index limit that capped practical numerical aperture in air, allowing NA above 1
It shortens the effective wavelength enough to skip a technology generation on its own
It cools the resist, reducing line-edge roughness
It increases the transmitted intensity, shortening exposure time

steps: Numerical aperture is $n\sin\theta$, and in air $n = 1$ bounds NA below one however good the lens.
The practical bound is tighter still, because rays beyond the critical angle at the lens-to-air interface are totally internally reflected and never reach the wafer.
Water at $n = 1.44$ is much closer to the lens glass at $n \approx 1.5$, so that interface stops rejecting high-angle rays.
That is what lets 193 nm immersion tools run at NA near 1.35, improving both resolution and — for a given feature — depth of focus.
explanation.principle: Immersion does not change the lens or the light. It changes the medium, and with it the largest angle the system can actually collect.
hints: What bounds NA when the medium is air?
What happens to rays beyond the critical angle?

items.stem: How does a phase-shift mask allow smaller features to be printed?

options.text: Adjacent apertures are made to transmit light 180° out of phase, so the fields cancel between them and the intensity minimum becomes sharp
It blocks the zeroth diffraction order, leaving only the higher orders to form the image
It shifts the focal plane to compensate for wafer non-flatness
It polarises the illumination so the resist absorbs more efficiently

steps: Diffraction spreads light from neighbouring apertures until their intensities overlap and the gap between features washes out.
A phase shifter in alternate apertures inverts the sign of the electric field emerging from them.
Where the two fields overlap they now cancel rather than add, and since resist responds to intensity — the square of the field — a true null appears between the features.
A sharper minimum means the printed features stay separate at pitches that would otherwise merge.
explanation.principle: The resist sees intensity, but the optics carry amplitude and phase. Controlling phase at the mask is a lever the intensity image alone does not offer.
hints: What does resist respond to — field or intensity?
What do two fields of opposite sign do where they overlap?

items.stem: What is the essential trade-off between contact and proximity printing?

options.text: Contact printing resolves finer features but damages the mask and generates defects; proximity printing spares the mask at the cost of resolution
Contact printing is faster but needs a brighter source
Proximity printing resolves better because the gap reduces diffraction
Contact printing works only with negative resist

steps: In shadow printing the resolvable feature scales roughly as $\sqrt{k\lambda g}$, so closing the gap $g$ improves resolution.
Hard contact drives $g$ toward zero and approaches the best resolution these systems can reach.
But repeatedly pressing a mask against resist-coated wafers scratches the mask and transfers particles, and a damaged mask prints its damage onto every subsequent wafer.
Proximity printing accepts a finite gap to protect the mask, and pays for it in resolution — which is why both were displaced by projection printing.
explanation.principle: Resolution and mask lifetime pull against each other in shadow printing, and projection optics exist to escape the choice entirely.
hints: What does the gap do to resolution?
What is the cost of a mask touching every wafer?

items.stem: MTF and CMTF are compared to decide whether a feature will print. Which is which?

options.text: MTF is the modulation of the optical image; CMTF is the modulation the resist needs, and the feature prints when MTF exceeds CMTF
MTF is a resist property and CMTF an optical one; the feature prints when CMTF exceeds MTF
Both are optical, measured before and after the resist stack
Both are resist properties, measured at two different doses

steps: The optical MTF is computed from the aerial image: $(I_{\max} - I_{\min})/(I_{\max} + I_{\min})$, a property of the projection system.
The resist CMTF is computed from the two dose limits: $(Q_f - Q_0)/(Q_f + Q_0)$, a property of the chemistry.
The resist can only distinguish exposed from unexposed if the image it receives is modulated by at least as much as it requires.
So the criterion is $\mathrm{MTF} > \mathrm{CMTF}$ — supply exceeding demand — and a high-contrast resist lowers the demand.
explanation.principle: One number describes what the optics deliver and one describes what the chemistry needs. The comparison is the whole resolution criterion.
hints: Which quantity is computed from intensities and which from doses?
Which side is supply and which is demand?

items.stem: A resist has a high contrast $\gamma$. What does that tell you about it?

options.text: It switches from unexposed to fully exposed over a narrow range of dose, so it discriminates sharply at the feature edge
It needs a high absolute dose to clear, so exposure times are long
It tolerates a wide range of doses before responding at all
It has a high refractive index at the exposure wavelength

steps: Contrast is $\gamma = 1/\log_{10}(Q_f/Q_0)$, so it is large when $Q_f$ and $Q_0$ are close together.
A narrow gap between "just starting to respond" and "fully cleared" means a small change in dose flips the resist.
At a feature edge the dose falls off gradually, and a sharp switch converts that gradual roll-off into a steep resist sidewall.
Contrast is independent of sensitivity: it is about the width of the transition, not where it sits on the dose axis.
explanation.principle: Contrast and sensitivity are separate axes. One is how sharply the resist switches; the other is how much light it takes.
hints: Does a high gamma mean Qf and Q0 are close together or far apart?
Is contrast about the position of the transition or its width?

items.stem: Raising the numerical aperture of a projection system improves resolution. What does it cost?

options.text: Depth of focus, which falls as $1/\mathrm{NA}^2$ and so degrades faster than resolution improves
Exposure dose, which must rise in proportion to NA
Field size, which shrinks in proportion to NA
Nothing — a higher NA is strictly better

steps: Resolution improves linearly: $R = k_1\lambda/\mathrm{NA}$.
Depth of focus degrades quadratically: $\mathrm{DOF} = \pm k_2\lambda/\mathrm{NA}^2$.
Doubling NA therefore halves the printable feature but quarters the usable focal range.

Since real depth of focus is already well under a micrometre, it is usually the binding constraint — which is why wafer flatness, resist thickness and focus control are lithography problems rather than afterthoughts.
explanation.principle: The two figures of merit share a parameter and move oppositely in it. That is the central trade of projection lithography.
hints: What power of NA appears in each expression?
Which of the two is usually the binding constraint?

items.stem: Why do resists for shorter exposure wavelengths need higher contrast than i-line resists did?

options.text: Smaller features have inherently lower optical image contrast, so the resist must supply more of the discrimination itself
Shorter wavelengths deposit less energy per photon, so the chemistry must compensate
Shorter wavelengths penetrate further into the resist, blurring the latent image
Shorter-wavelength sources are less stable, so the resist must tolerate dose variation

steps: As features approach the resolution limit, the aerial image degrades: $I_{\max}$ falls and $I_{\min}$ rises, so the optical MTF drops.
The resolution criterion $\mathrm{MTF} > \mathrm{CMTF}$ still has to be satisfied.
With less MTF available from the optics, the only way to keep the inequality is to lower CMTF, which means raising resist contrast.
That is why contrast climbed from around 2–3 for i-line resists to 5–10 for DUV, and higher again for EUV.
explanation.principle: When the optics give less contrast, the chemistry must demand less. The resolution criterion is a budget shared between them.
hints: What happens to the aerial image as features approach the limit?
Which side of the inequality can chemistry change?

items.stem: Crystalline silicon has a diamond cubic structure with a lattice parameter of 5.43 Å and eight atoms per unit cell. Roughly how many silicon atoms occupy a cubic centimetre?

options.text: About $5 \times 10^{22}$
About $5 \times 10^{19}$
About $8 \times 10^{23}$, one Avogadro number per cell
About $1 \times 10^{15}$, the typical doping level

steps: The unit cell is a cube of side $a = 5.43\ \mathrm{\AA} = 5.43 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}$.
Its volume is $a^3 = 1.6 \times 10^{-22}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, and it contains eight atoms.
Dividing gives $8 / (1.6 \times 10^{-22}) \approx 5 \times 10^{22}$ atoms per cubic centimetre.
This number is worth deriving once and then knowing: it is the denominator whenever a dose or a consumed thickness has to be turned into an atom count.
explanation.principle: A lattice parameter and an atoms-per-cell count determine the density completely. Everything else in doping is measured against it.
hints: What is the volume of the unit cell in cubic centimetres?
How many atoms does each cell hold?

items.stem: A wafer doped at $10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ is often called heavily doped in casual conversation. Compared with the silicon itself, what fraction of lattice sites is that?

options.text: About two in ten million — doping is a tiny perturbation of an almost pure crystal
About one in a hundred
About one in a thousand
Roughly half, since the dopant must outnumber intrinsic carriers

steps: Silicon has about $5 \times 10^{22}$ atoms per cubic centimetre.
A doping level of $10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ is therefore $10^{16}/(5 \times 10^{22}) = 2 \times 10^{-7}$ of the atoms present.
That is two parts in ten million, and even a degenerate $10^{20}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ implant is only two parts in a thousand.
This is why contamination targets are so severe: an unintended impurity at a level that would be invisible in most materials is comparable to the deliberate doping here.
explanation.principle: Doping changes the electrical behaviour of silicon completely while barely changing its composition. That sensitivity is exactly why the cleanroom exists.
hints: How many silicon atoms are there to compare against?
What does that ratio imply about tolerable contamination?

items.stem: What distinguishes an integrated device manufacturer from a pure-play foundry?

options.text: An IDM designs and manufactures its own products; a pure-play foundry manufactures to other companies' designs and sells no chips of its own
An IDM owns its fabs while a foundry leases capacity from others
An IDM makes memory and a foundry makes logic
An IDM operates at leading-edge nodes and a foundry at trailing ones

steps: The distinction is about which parts of the value chain a company occupies, not about the equipment it owns.
An integrated device manufacturer does both design and manufacturing in house, and sells the resulting parts.
A pure-play foundry manufactures only, to designs its customers supply, and competes by not competing with those customers.
A fabless company is the complement: it designs and sells but owns no manufacturing at all.
explanation.principle: The business model determines what a company can be trusted with, which is why the pure-play model exists at all.
hints: Who owns the design in each case?
Does the company sell chips under its own name?

items.stem: Modern process node names such as "3 nm" or "18 A" do not correspond to any physical dimension on the chip. What do they track?

options.text: Generational density improvements in the spirit of Moore's law, achieved largely through three-dimensional structures rather than shrinking gate length
The thinnest gate oxide in the process
The minimum metal pitch of the lowest interconnect layer
The physical gate length, which is still measured directly

steps: Under Dennard scaling the node name really was the gate length, and each generation shrank it by about $0.7\times$.
That correspondence broke once planar scaling ran out and density came instead from FinFET and gate-all-around structures.
The names continued as commercial labels for equivalent density gains, so a "3 nm" process contains nothing that measures 3 nm.
This is why comparing nodes between foundries by name alone is meaningless — the useful comparisons are transistor density and performance per watt.
explanation.principle: A name that once measured something and now markets something is a common pattern in this industry, and knowing which is which is part of reading a roadmap.
hints: Did the name ever correspond to a real dimension?
What replaced planar shrinking as the source of density?

items.stem: Phosphorus is introduced into silicon. What does it contribute, and what type of material results?

options.text: It donates a conduction electron, producing n-type silicon
It accepts an electron, leaving a hole and producing p-type silicon
It donates a hole, producing n-type silicon
It is electrically neutral and only strains the lattice

steps: Silicon sits in group IV and forms four covalent bonds with its neighbours.
Phosphorus is group V, so when it substitutes for a silicon atom it has one valence electron left over after bonding.
That electron is only weakly bound and enters the conduction band at room temperature, making the material n-type.
The group III elements — boron most commonly — are the mirror image: one bond short, leaving a hole and making the material p-type.
explanation.principle: The group number relative to silicon's four is the whole rule. Group V donates, group III accepts.
hints: How many valence electrons does phosphorus have?
How many bonds does it need to make?

items.stem: Silicon dioxide is used as a mask against dopant diffusion. What has to be true for that to work for a particular dopant?

options.text: The dopant must diffuse much more slowly in the oxide than in silicon, so the oxide is thick enough to stop it within the process time
The dopant must be chemically unable to enter the oxide at all
The oxide must be thicker than the intended junction depth
The dopant must be an interstitial rather than a substitutional diffuser

steps: Masking is a race, not a wall: the question is whether the dopant crosses the oxide before the process ends.
Boron, phosphorus, arsenic and antimony all diffuse far more slowly in $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ than in silicon, so a modest oxide thickness stops them.
Gallium and indium do not follow that pattern and pass through oxide much more readily, which is why oxide is not a general-purpose dopant mask.
The required thickness therefore depends on the dopant, the temperature and the duration together, not on the junction depth.
explanation.principle: A diffusion mask works on a rate comparison over a fixed time. Whether it works at all is a property of the dopant, not of the mask.
hints: Is the dopant stopped, or merely slowed?
Does the same oxide mask every dopant equally well?

items.stem: Why is airflow in a cleanroom directed downward in a laminar pattern rather than simply circulated?

options.text: Unidirectional downward flow carries particles away from wafers and out through the floor before they can settle
Laminar flow reduces the energy needed to move the same volume of air
Turbulent flow would heat the room beyond process tolerance
Downward flow keeps the room at positive pressure

steps: Filtration removes particles from the supply air, but people and tools generate particles continuously inside the room.
Turbulent circulation would keep those particles suspended and give them many chances to land on a wafer.
Unidirectional downward flow gives each particle one short, predictable path: from where it was generated, straight down, and out.
That is also why wafers are handled below the airflow rather than above it, and why an operator leaning over an open cassette is a defect mechanism.
explanation.principle: Filtration controls what enters the room; airflow direction controls what happens to whatever is generated inside it.
hints: Where do particles inside a cleanroom come from?
What would turbulence do to a particle's path?

items.stem: Why was the FS209 cleanroom classification replaced by the ISO 14644 scheme?

options.text: FS209 counted particles at a single 0.5 µm threshold, which cannot express control of the much smaller particles modern nodes care about
FS209 was a United States standard and ISO is international, with no technical difference
FS209 measured particles per cubic foot and the industry moved to metric units
FS209 classes were too coarse at the dirty end of the range

steps: An FS209 class number was the count of particles of 0.5 µm and larger per cubic foot of air.
As critical defect sizes fell well below that, two rooms with identical FS209 classes could differ enormously in the particles that actually mattered.
ISO 14644 specifies cumulative concentration limits across a range of particle sizes, so a class constrains the small end as well.
The change of units is real but incidental; the substantive change is that the classification now says something about the sizes that kill modern die.
explanation.principle: A specification is only useful while it constrains the quantity that matters. When the critical size moved, the old metric stopped discriminating.
hints: What single size did FS209 measure?
Is that the size that kills a modern die?

items.stem: Which RCA step removes organic residues and photoresist, and what makes it work?

options.text: The sulphuric acid and hydrogen peroxide mixture, because peroxide is a strong enough oxidiser to break organic molecules apart
The dilute HF step, because HF dissolves carbon-containing films
The SC-2 hydrochloric step, because acid hydrolyses the polymer
The DI water rinse with ultrasonic agitation, which dislodges them mechanically

steps: Organic contamination — resist residue, skin oils, packaging films — is held together by carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen bonds.
Breaking those requires oxidation, and the sulphuric-peroxide mixture is an aggressive oxidiser at 120 to 150 °C.
HF strips oxide and leaves organics untouched; SC-2 targets alkali ions and metals.
This is the general shape of the RCA sequence: each bath is chosen for one contaminant class, and running them in the wrong order wastes the chemistry.
explanation.principle: Each step in the clean is matched to a bond type. Knowing what holds a contaminant on tells you what will take it off.
hints: What kind of bonds hold an organic film together?
Which bath is the strong oxidiser?

items.stem: Why is deionised water manufactured on site at a fab rather than delivered?

options.text: Water picks up ions from any container or pipe it sits in, so purity degrades in storage and transport and must be produced where it is used
The volumes involved make transport uneconomic
Deionised water is classified as hazardous in transport
Municipal water is already pure enough and only needs filtering at the point of use

steps: Ultrapure water is an aggressive solvent precisely because it has nothing dissolved in it.
It leaches ions from pipework, tanks and the air, so resistivity falls continuously once production stops.
Fabs therefore run continuous polishing loops that recirculate water through ion exchange and keep it at specification right up to the point of use.
Volume is genuinely large as well, but the controlling reason is that purity cannot be preserved in storage.
explanation.principle: Some specifications cannot be met by a product and then kept; they have to be maintained continuously. Ultrapure water is the clearest example in the fab.
hints: What happens to pure water sitting in a tank?
Why is pure water such an effective solvent?

items.stem: A fab observes that defects on its wafers are not randomly scattered but appear in recognisable spatial patterns. What does that usually indicate?

options.text: A specific tool or handling step is responsible, and the pattern is a signature that points at it
The wafers were measured incorrectly, since real defects are random by definition
The defect density is too low for randomness to be visible
The wafer was misaligned during inspection

steps: Random scatter is what a defect distribution looks like when many independent small sources contribute.

A pattern means one source dominates, and its geometry usually identifies it: edge rings from handling or edge-bead removal, radial streaks from spin coating, clusters from a chuck, repeating shapes from a reticle field.
This is why defect maps are read visually as well as counted — the count says how bad, the pattern says what.
It is also the physical basis for clustering in the yield models: real defect sources are localised, which is what the negative binomial's clustering factor encodes.
explanation.principle: The spatial arrangement of defects carries information the total count destroys. That is also why Poisson, which assumes it away, is the pessimistic model.
hints: What would produce a ring at the wafer edge?
How does this connect to the clustering factor?

items.stem: Automotive-grade silicon is specified at under one defective part per million, while a novelty toy may tolerate more than ten thousand. What drives the difference?

options.text: The cost and consequence of a field failure, which ranges from replacing a cheap item to a safety recall
Automotive parts are physically larger and so need tighter defect control
Automotive parts run at higher temperatures, which exposes more defects
Consumer parts are tested less thoroughly, so their true rate is unknown

steps: Defects per million is a specification on parts that escape to the customer, not on manufacturing yield.
What sets the acceptable level is what a single escape costs: a toy is replaced for a few dollars, an airbag controller or braking sensor can mean a recall and a safety investigation.
That economic asymmetry is why automotive-qualified lines run tighter process control, more burn-in and more screening than consumer lines on the same equipment.
It is also why the same die can be sold into two markets at different grades after different amounts of test.
explanation.principle: Quality targets are set by the cost of failure, not by what the process can manage. The process is then built to reach the target.
hints: What does a single escaped defect cost in each case?
Is this a statement about yield or about escapes?

items.stem: Raising the oxidation pressure increases the growth rate. Which part of the Deal-Grove model does that act on?

options.text: The equilibrium oxidant concentration $C^{*}$, which by Henry's law rises with partial pressure and raises both $B$ and $B/A$
The diffusivity $D$ alone, so only the parabolic constant changes
The reaction rate $k_s$ alone, so only the linear constant changes
The fictitious time offset $\tau$, which shrinks with pressure

steps: Henry's law makes the dissolved oxidant concentration proportional to its partial pressure above the film.
$C^{*}$ appears in both rate constants: $B = 2DC^{*}/N_1$ and $B/A = k_sC^{*}/N_1$.
So raising pressure scales both, and the growth rate rises in every regime rather than only in one.
The practical value is thermal budget: about an extra atmosphere buys roughly 30 °C of temperature reduction at the same rate, which means less unwanted dopant diffusion elsewhere on the wafer.
explanation.principle: A parameter that appears in both rate constants changes the whole curve. Knowing where a variable enters the model tells you which regime it affects.
hints: Where does $C^*$ appear in the two rate constants?
What is the practical reason to trade pressure for temperature?

items.stem: Why is gettering effectiveness strongly metal-dependent, working well for copper and poorly for titanium?

options.text: The mechanism relies on the contaminant diffusing to a trap site, and diffusivities differ by orders of magnitude between metals
Titanium is chemically inert and forms no bond with trap sites
Copper is present at lower concentrations, so its traps never saturate
Titanium is a lighter atom and is not held by lattice strain

steps: Gettering has three steps, and the middle one is ordinary diffusion toward a sink.
Copper and interstitial gold are extremely fast diffusers in silicon and reach trap sites easily within a normal thermal step.
Titanium diffuses slowly, so within the same time and temperature much of it never arrives.
The remedy is not a better trap but a different contamination strategy — for slow diffusers, keeping the metal out is the only approach that works.
explanation.principle: When a mechanism depends on transport, its effectiveness inherits the spread in transport rates. That spread is enormous for metals in silicon.
hints: Which of the three gettering steps depends on the specific metal?
What should be done instead for a slow diffuser?

items.stem: A thermally oxidised wafer shows a distinct colour under white light that changes with oxide thickness. What produces it?

options.text: Thin-film interference between light reflected from the oxide surface and from the oxide-silicon interface, which cancels some wavelengths
Absorption bands in $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ that shift with thickness
Scattering from the roughness of the oxide surface
Fluorescence of the oxide under ambient illumination

steps: Light reaching the wafer partly reflects at the top of the oxide and partly travels through it and reflects at the silicon beneath.
The two reflections recombine with a path difference set by the oxide thickness and its refractive index.
Wavelengths that meet the destructive condition are removed from the reflected light, and what remains is the colour seen.
That is also why the colour repeats through several orders as the film thickens, and why a colour chart is only useful when the approximate thickness is already known.
explanation.principle: The colour is a measurement, not a property of the material. It encodes an optical path length, which is thickness times index.
hints: How many reflections does the eye receive?
Why does the same colour recur at several thicknesses?

items.stem: A wafer is measured by colour chart and reported as 100 nm of oxide. What is the main risk in that measurement?

options.text: Interference colours repeat in higher orders, so a much thicker film can show the same colour
Colour charts are only calibrated for wet oxides
The colour depends on the doping of the substrate underneath
Colour charts cannot resolve films thinner than a micrometre

steps: The destructive condition is met whenever the optical path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths, which happens repeatedly as thickness grows.
So a given colour corresponds to a family of thicknesses, not to one.
A colour reading is therefore only unambiguous when the order is already known from the process, which it usually is.
Reflectometry and ellipsometry resolve the ambiguity properly by fitting across a range of wavelengths rather than judging one perceived colour.
explanation.principle: An ambiguous measurement is safe only while something else pins down which branch you are on. Saying what that something is, is part of quoting the result.
hints: Does one colour correspond to exactly one thickness?
What extra information resolves it?

items.stem: What are the eight steps of a photolithography module, in order?

options.text: Vapour prime, spin coat, soft bake, align and expose, post-exposure bake, develop, hard bake, develop inspect
Spin coat, vapour prime, soft bake, align and expose, develop, post-exposure bake, hard bake, inspect
Vapour prime, spin coat, align and expose, soft bake, post-exposure bake, develop, inspect, hard bake
Vapour prime, spin coat, soft bake, align and expose, develop, post-exposure bake, hard bake, inspect

steps: The prime comes first because it changes the surface chemistry so resist will adhere; applying it afterwards would do nothing.
The soft bake drives off solvent so the film is stable enough to expose; it has to precede exposure.
The post-exposure bake sits between exposure and develop, which is what makes chemical amplification possible — the acid generated at exposure needs heat before the pattern is developed away.
The hard bake follows develop and toughens the remaining resist for whatever etch or implant it will mask, and the inspection closes the loop before the wafer moves on.
explanation.principle: The order is forced by what each step needs from the one before it. A step in the wrong place is not merely inefficient; it usually does nothing at all.
hints: Why must the prime precede the coat?
Where must the post-exposure bake sit for amplification to work?

items.stem: What usually happens to a wafer immediately after the lithography module completes?

options.text: Etch or ion implantation, using the patterned resist as the mask that the whole module existed to create
Another lithography step to add the complementary pattern
Thermal oxidation, which the resist survives
Metrology alone, since resist patterns are inspected and then stripped

steps: Lithography does not modify the wafer in any lasting way; it produces a patterned polymer film.
The value of that film is entirely in what it blocks: etchant from the regions to be preserved, or ions from the regions not to be doped.
So the step after develop inspect is the one the mask was made for, and the resist is stripped once it has done its job.
It cannot be oxidation: an organic resist would simply burn off at the several hundred degrees oxidation requires.
explanation.principle: Lithography is never the point. It is the step that makes a subsequent selective step possible, which is why the mask exists.
hints: What does the patterned resist physically do?
Would resist survive a furnace?

items.stem: How does annular or off-axis illumination improve resolution?

options.text: It illuminates the mask at an angle so both the zeroth and first diffraction orders fall inside the lens aperture, which lowers the achievable $k_1$
It concentrates more energy into the same area, shortening exposure
It reduces the effective wavelength of the illumination
It removes the zeroth order entirely, leaving a sharper image

steps: Forming an image of a periodic pattern needs at least two diffraction orders to interfere at the wafer.
With on-axis illumination the first order can fall outside the aperture for a fine pitch, leaving only the zeroth order and no image at all.
Tilting the illumination shifts the whole diffraction pattern so the zeroth and one first order both fit inside the aperture.
Nothing about the lens or the wavelength has changed; what has changed is which orders are collected, and that shows up as a smaller usable $k_1$.
explanation.principle: Resolution enhancement techniques mostly work by changing what the existing optics collect, rather than by improving the optics.
hints: How many diffraction orders are needed to form an image?
What does tilting the illumination do to where those orders land?

items.stem: What is the main disadvantage of immersion lithography?

options.text: The water introduces a new defect mechanism — bubbles, watermarks and particles carried in the fluid — and constrains scan speed
It cannot be used with chemically amplified resists
It requires a shorter wavelength source than dry lithography
It reduces depth of focus compared with a dry system at the same NA

steps: Immersion buys a higher practical numerical aperture and, for a given feature, better depth of focus than a dry tool would give.
What it costs is a liquid in contact with the resist during exposure, moving at scan speed.
Bubbles scatter light, watermarks leave residue, and any particle in the fluid is delivered directly to the wafer, so water purity and flow control become yield-critical.
The resist also has to tolerate contact with water without leaching its photo-acid generator, which drove the development of topcoat layers.
explanation.principle: A technique that improves one axis usually introduces a new failure mode rather than none. Knowing the cost is what makes the trade real.
hints: What is now physically touching the resist during exposure?
Does immersion help or hurt depth of focus?
